title: INC-2026-006: Contractor access key c.ng used from an unfamiliar IP to self-grant AdministratorAccess and launch GPU instances
severity_rationale: The c.ng account was compromised and the actor attached AdministratorAccess, created a key for svc.reporting and launched 4 GPU instances. Responders contained this by deactivating keys, detaching the policy and terminating the instances. No large-scale sensitive data exposure is confirmed. Management events show ListBuckets only, but object reads cannot be ruled out because S3 data-event logging was off.
executive_summary: c.ng was used from an IP not previously seen for the account and attached AdministratorAccess to itself. The same session created an access key for svc.reporting and launched 4 large GPU instances. c.ng's access key was found in a public repository commit. The misuse was probably done with that leaked key, but this is not confirmed. The contractors group's CI deploy policy granted iam:*, so any member could self-escalate. Long-lived contractor keys were also permitted. The admin-policy alert went to email only. On-call was paged only by the later GPU launch alert. Keys were deactivated, the admin policy detached and the instances terminated. Data reads cannot be ruled out because S3 data-event logging was off.

lessons.lesson: Broad IAM permissions on a shared contractor group let one leaked credential escalate to full administrator. Only the cloud administrators group should hold iam:* and policy-attachment rights, and permission boundaries should block self-attachment.

evidence.excerpt: grants iam:* so any member could attach AdministratorAccess to themselves

policy_refs.excerpt: The iam:* permission and policy-attachment rights are granted only to the cloud administrators group

lessons.lesson: A 400-day-old long-lived contractor key allowed a leaked credential to be used long after it was created. Policy prohibits such keys.

evidence.excerpt: c.ng's key was 400 days old

policy_refs.title: Cloud credentials
policy_refs.excerpt: Long-lived access keys are prohibited for human and contractor users

lessons.lesson: Alerting on privilege escalation must reach a human immediately. The email-only admin-policy alert delayed response until the GPU alert paged on-call.

lessons.lesson: Missing S3 data-event logging left the data-exposure question unanswerable. Required log sources must be enabled for buckets with confidential data.

corrective_actions.recommendation: Remove iam:* from the contractors group CI deploy policy. Restrict iam:* and policy attachment to the cloud administrators group and enforce permission boundaries.
corrective_actions.reason: Any member of the contractors group could attach AdministratorAccess to themselves.

supporting_evidence.excerpt: grants iam:* so any member could attach AdministratorAccess to themselves

corrective_actions.expected_benefit: A compromised contractor identity can no longer escalate itself to administrator.

policy_refs.title: Cloud credentials
policy_refs.excerpt: permission boundaries must stop users attaching administrative policies to themselves

corrective_actions.recommendation: Replace long-lived access keys for contractors with short-lived SSO credentials. Rotate or remove any remaining old keys, starting with keys older than 90 days.
corrective_actions.reason: c.ng's 400-day-old key was exposed publicly and then used.
corrective_actions.expected_benefit: Leaked credentials expire quickly and have less value.

policy_refs.title: Cloud credentials
policy_refs.excerpt: it must be rotated within 90 days

corrective_actions.recommendation: Route the admin-policy-attached alert (and similar IAM privilege-change alerts) to paging, not email only.
corrective_actions.reason: The 01:13 admin-policy alert went to email only and on-call was paged only by the later GPU alert.

supporting_evidence.excerpt: The admin-policy alert at 01:13 went to email only.

corrective_actions.expected_benefit: Faster response to privilege escalation in cloud accounts.

corrective_actions.recommendation: Enable S3 data-event logging for buckets holding confidential or restricted data. Keep logs for at least one year.

corrective_actions.recommendation: Complete a persistence review of every c.ng action. Delete (not only deactivate) the key created for svc.reporting and remove anything else the actor created.

corrective_actions.expected_benefit: No attacker foothold remains in the account.

corrective_actions.recommendation: Remove the leaked key from repository history, rotate every credential found there and enable push-time secret scanning.

open_questions: Who committed the key to the public repository, and was it committed intentionally or by mistake?
Which key authenticated the activity from 198.51.100.77? Records link it to the leaked key only by inference.
Were any objects read from the enumerated buckets, and what is the data classification of those buckets?
What was the purpose of the 4 GPU instances (for example, whether they were used for resource abuse)? The evidence does not say.
Was every c.ng action in the cloud account reviewed for other persistence beyond the svc.reporting key?
remaining_risks: The leaked key may remain in public repository history until it is purged, and other credentials committed there may be exposed.
The contractors group CI deploy policy still grants iam:* until it is corrected. No fix is recorded.
Data exposure cannot be ruled out until storage access is assessed, because object-level logs do not exist.
The svc.reporting key was deactivated, but its deletion and any other persistence are not recorded.
